UrbanMart Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the UrbanMart Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss UrbanMart Inc.'s results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today’s call are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Mike Rivera, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Sarah Thompson.

Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report UrbanMart Inc.'s performance for the Q3 2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover four key aspects of our performance. First, our omnichannel initiatives have made significant strides, driving revenue growth and customer loyalty. Second, we've seen meaningful improvements in our inventory turnover ratio, reflecting operational discipline. Third, supply chain efficiencies are yielding substantial cost savings and better availability. And fourth, our store remodel and renovation plans are transforming our physical footprint into high-performing assets.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Rivera to provide more details on our financial results and expand on these areas.

Mike Rivera, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3 2024.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $4.8 billion, a 4.2% increase compared to the same period last year, fueled by comp store sales growth of 4.2% and strength in omnichannel channels. Gross margin was 38.5%, primarily driven by omnichannel mix shift, reduced markdowns, and supply chain cost reductions. Operating expenses were $1.65 billion, representing 34.4% of revenue, as we balanced investments in remodels and digital with disciplined cost controls. Net income was $285 million, or $1.65 per share. We generated $520 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels are currently optimized at $1.2 billion at quarter-end, down 8% year-over-year, supporting our improved turnover metrics.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Let me now expand on the key aspects Sarah highlighted, starting with our omnichannel initiatives, which continue to be a cornerstone of our strategy at UrbanMart Inc. to deliver frictionless customer experiences across our 1,200 brick-and-mortar locations nationwide. Omnichannel isn't just a buzzword for us—it's a proven driver of revenue growth, margin expansion, and customer loyalty in an industry where pure-play e-commerce giants like Amazon are squeezing traditional retailers. Our focus on Buy Online Pick-Up In Store, or BOPIS, curbside pickup, and ship-from-store has accelerated post-pandemic, with omnichannel sales representing 28% of our total digital revenue in Q3, up from 19% a year ago—that's a robust 47% year-over-year increase to $1.2 billion.

Breaking this down, BOPIS fulfillment hit a record 2.5 million orders in the quarter, up 35% year-over-year, accounting for 62% of all store-fulfilled digital orders. This outperformed our internal target of 30% growth and beats industry benchmarks, such as Target's 40% omnichannel penetration or Walmart's pickup dominance. The average BOPIS basket size was $145, 22% higher than our pure e-commerce average of $119, thanks to targeted upsell algorithms in the app that suggest complementary in-store exclusives like our private-label UrbanHome kitchenware line. Conversion rates from app reservations to completed pickups stayed at 92%, with fulfillment times averaging under 2 hours in 85% of stores—a direct result of our $150 million investment last year in real-time inventory synchronization via our proprietary UrbanSync platform, powered by Manhattan Associates' warehouse management system and integrated with our legacy POS from NCR.

Curbside pickup, our contactless flagship, showed even stronger momentum: 1.8 million orders, up 52% year-over-year, driven by ongoing consumer preferences for safety and convenience amid softening e-commerce growth rates, which NRF data pegs at just 8-10% for 2024. This channel now drives 18% of digital sales, with a 95% on-time fulfillment rate. Basket uplift here is impressive at 28% over pure delivery, as customers often add impulse buys during the pickup window—like our seasonal grilling essentials or apparel add-ons. Marginally, curbside yields a 12-point gross margin advantage over home delivery, thanks to zero last-mile shipping costs and minimal packaging waste.

Regionally, performance trends positively across the board. In our high-density urban markets—the Northeast Corridor and California, representing 45% of stores—omnichannel penetration exceeds 35%, fueled by tech-savvy millennials and Gen Z who make up 55% of BOPIS users per our customer analytics. For instance, our flagship store in Manhattan saw BOPIS volumes spike 68% year-over-year, correlating with a 15% lift in adjacent-category foot traffic for beauty and electronics. In the Sunbelt and Midwest heartland, like Texas and Ohio clusters accounting for 30% of stores, curbside grew 65% year-over-year as rural and suburban families prioritize time savings amid inflation pressures. Even in softer Southeast markets, where apparel comps lagged at +2%, omnichannel drove a 12% store traffic increase, countering the 5-7% industry-wide traffic decline reported by Placer.ai.

On the technical side, we've added geofencing to our mobile app, now with 18 million active users up 24% year-over-year, for hyper-local inventory visibility—the "endless aisle" effect—allowing real-time reservations from nearby stores. We've expanded ship-from-store to 95% of locations, fulfilling 25% of online orders this way, boosting in-store inventory turns by 18% and reducing central DC logistics costs by 15%. Partnerships include deeper integration with Instacart for marketplace BOPIS in 400 stores and piloting RFID tagging with Avery Dennison in 50 high-volume locations to cut pick accuracy errors to under 0.5%. Backend, our AI-driven demand forecasting via Blue Yonder has improved omnichannel stock availability to 97%, minimizing the industry-wide $2.5 billion in lost sales from out-of-stocks that Deloitte highlights.

These efforts are reshaping our P&L. Omnichannel sales grew at 2.5x the rate of pure e-commerce and delivered 450 basis points of gross margin expansion quarter-over-quarter, versus 34% for delivery-heavy channels. This leverages our 45 million square feet of prime real estate as micro-fulfillment centers, much like Best Buy's model that propelled their omnichannel to 27% of sales. Customer lifetime value for omnichannel shoppers is 3.2x higher than single-channel, with 68% repeat purchase rates within 30 days, per our Loyalty360 data. Amid macroeconomic headwinds—persistent 3-4% comp deflation in apparel and softening consumer sentiment at 85 on the Conference Board index—we're using omnichannel to halo our stores: pickup customers spend 35% more in-store on unplanned items, driving overall store comps to +4.2%.

Looking forward, we're allocating $200 million from capex toward omnichannel in FY25, including a 200-store rollout of automated micro-fulfillment lockers similar to Walmart's Alphabot and app-based scan-and-go for in-store pickups. We expect omnichannel to reach 35% of digital sales by year-end, contributing 150 basis points to overall EPS accretion. This positions UrbanMart to capture share in a $1.1 trillion U.S. retail market where McKinsey projects hybrid shopping to grow at 15% CAGR through 2027.

Next, let's discuss our inventory turnover ratio, a key operating metric in the brick-and-mortar retail space. For context, it's calculated as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory levels, showing how efficiently we cycle through stock. In our industry, where shelf space is limited, markdowns erode margins, and out-of-stocks push customers to competitors like Amazon or TJX Companies, a higher turnover is a hallmark of excellence. Our target is north of 5.5x annualized for core apparel and home categories, aligning with best-in-class peers like Ross Stores at around 6.2x LTM, while broader department store players like Macy's are in the 4.0x to 4.5x range.

For Q3 2024, our inventory turnover was 1.42x on a quarterly basis, annualizing to approximately 5.7x. This is a 10% improvement year-over-year from 1.29x or 5.2x annualized in Q3 2023. Average inventory at quarter-end was $1.2 billion, down 8% from last year, while COGS grew modestly amid softer comps in discretionary categories. This efficiency contributed to our gross margin expansion, as markdowns fell to 18% of sales from 22% last year, and shrinkage stayed under 1.2% through better loss prevention tech.

By category, apparel led with 6.1x annualized turnover, driven by fast-fashion pods in 450 stores—think trendy denim and activewear from Levi's and Lululemon partnerships, turning 4.2x quarterly. Home goods were at 4.8x annualized, reflecting softer demand for big-ticket items amid high interest rates, but we improved 15% year-over-year by rightsizing SKUs from 2,500 to 1,800 per store cluster. Footwear held at 5.9x, benefiting from exclusive Nike and Adidas collaborations.

We've seen steady improvement: Q1 at 5.1x annualized up 5% YoY, Q2 at 5.3x up 8%, Q3 at 5.7x up 10%. Post-COVID, while peers like Kohl's and Nordstrom carried excess inventory into 2023 due to Red Sea disruptions and port congestion, we clawed back aggressively.

Regionally, Sunbelt—Texas, Florida, Southeast, 35% of stores—led at 6.3x annualized, with +4.2% Q3 comps from seasonal apparel cycles and migration trends. Northeast and Midwest were at 5.0x, impacted by winters and inflation on lower-income households, with higher markdowns on outerwear in Rust Belt stores. Our 150 Canadian doors hit 5.2x, optimized by localized assortments from our Toronto DC.

Driving this are tech investments for omnichannel, where BOPIS is 28% of sales. We rolled out RFID on 80% of apparel SKUs with Avery Dennison, slashing scan times 40% and boosting turnover 0.3x in those categories. AI forecasting via Blue Yonder integrates POS, weather, and macro signals, hitting 92% accuracy at store-SKU level, cutting safety stock 12% without stockouts over 3%.

Supply chain efforts include dual-sourcing 70% of imports from Vietnam and Mexico, locking vendor rebates tied to turnover, saving $45 million in COGS. Micro-fulfillment pilots in 20 urban stores turn e-comm inventory 8x faster.

Every 0.1x turnover gain frees $25 million in working capital for remodels and dividends. We guide FY24 to 5.6x-5.9x, with private label at 25% of sales turning 7.2x as a buffer.

Turning to supply chain efficiency improvements, these gains are mission-critical in an industry with razor-thin 2-4% margins, battling Red Sea issues, Long Beach congestion, and ocean freight up 20-30% YoY per Drewry. They bolstered EBITDA margins by 120 basis points and on-shelf availability to 96.5% from 92%, fueling 4.2% comp growth.

Top-line, optimizations cut stockouts 28% across 1,200 stores, lifting units per transaction 15% in apparel and electronics, adding $450 million in revenue from avoided lost sales per our Nielsen-calibrated models.

Costs dropped to 8.1% of sales from 9.7%, a 160 bps gain, via 22% lower freight per unit. Inventory days outstanding improved to 52 from 68, pushing turns to 7.0x from 5.4x, nearing Home Depot's 7.5x. Inventory ended at $1.2 billion, down 12% YoY despite 5% sales growth.

Our $250 million digital transformation over 18 months yields 4.5x ROI. Core is AI demand sensing on Manhattan WMS and Blue Yonder, using 1.2 petabytes of POS, weather, and loyalty data from 45 million members—forecast accuracy to 92% at SKU-store-week, cutting safety stock 18%.

Fulfillment MFCs in 8 high-density markets, with AutoStore and Symbotic automation, cut last-mile costs 35% for ship-from-store, handling 25% omnichannel volume at 99.8% pick accuracy and 1,200 lines/hour. This supports store replenishment, reducing truckloads via VMI with P&G and Unilever on 40% CPG SKUs.

Regionally, U.S. (78% footprint) nearshoring 25% apparel to Mexico cut lead times to 21 days, duties 8%, with supplier scorecards for 15% lower costs and 97% on-time. Europe (15%) consolidated UK DCs to two via DHL, cutting freight 19%. Asia-Pacific (7%) dual-sourced Bangladesh amid Vietnam typhoons, holding DIO at 48 vs. industry 65.

This supports "Stores First, Digital Everywhere"—85% sales in stores per Placer.ai—with stores as nodes for 60% same-day BOPIS, expanding gross margins 2.5%. FY25 targets 10-15% more cuts via IBM Food Trust blockchain for perishables and TuSimple autonomous trucks.

With $1.2 billion capex including three new DCs, we're resilient for 12-15% EBITDA margins and 150 net new stores in suburbs.

Finally, our store remodel and renovation plans are a high-ROI cornerstone of 'Stores of the Future,' fortifying brick-and-mortar against e-commerce while boosting omnichannel. FY24 capex is $450 million, 65% or $292.5 million to remodels—up 25% from $234 million last year. We've completed 85 in H1, on track for 220 or 18% of 1,200 stores, at $1.35 million average, down 8% via supply chain gains and bulk fixtures from Steelcase and Herman Miller.

Modular tiers by performance:

Tier 1 high-volume flagships (45 stores, top 20% AUV at $25 million): $2.1 million each for experiential zones—AR smart mirrors from Meta (92% size accuracy, +12% apparel conversion), BOPIS hubs with RFID (-35% out-of-stocks). Post-remodel comps +7.2%, dwell time +22% per RetailNext.

Tier 2 mid-tier (120 stores, suburban): $1.2 million for 60/30/10 layout—open merchandising with Nike/Levi's shops, digital signage with AI personalization, backroom MFCs (+18% services revenue). 80% recycled fixtures for LEED Silver, appealing to Gen Z.

Tier 3 value refresh (55 stores, rural): $850,000 with IKEA racking, NCR self-checkout (-15% labor), LiDAR for HVAC (-22% energy amid +11% utility hikes).

Northeast (35% remodels): luxury pop-ups like Sephora (+9% comps from tourism). Midwest (40%): value endcaps, loyalty kiosks (+5.4% frequency vs. industry -1.2% SSS). West Coast (25%): solar roofing, zero-waste for +28% eco-comps.

ROI averages 3.2x over three years, +5.8% SSS year one scaling to +9.1%, +110 bps margins from higher ASPs and OpEx leverage. Financed by $620 million FCF and $300 million green bond.

FY25 capex to $500 million for 300 remodels with AWS edge-computing, holding brick-and-mortar at 65% of $1.2 trillion market per McKinsey.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of persistent inflation on your sales mix?

Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Inflation continues to pressure discretionary categories like apparel, where we've seen 3-4% comp deflation, but our omnichannel initiatives have been a strong counterbalance. BOPIS and curbside customers are spending 35% more on unplanned in-store items, driving overall comps to +4.2%. Supply chain efficiencies and inventory discipline have kept pricing power intact, minimizing markdowns to 18% of sales. We're seeing resilience in urban markets and Sunbelt regions, where traffic is up.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Jane Doe with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Jane Doe (Morgan Stanley):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Mike Rivera, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Jane. We're guiding Q4 same-store sales growth to 3.5% to 5.0%, assuming stable consumer sentiment and no major disruptions. This factors in remodel momentum—post-renovation stores are at +7.2% comps—continued omnichannel at 30%+ of digital, and inventory turns holding 5.7x annualized. Supply chain tailwinds should add another 50-75 bps to margins.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Alex Patel with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Alex Patel (JPMorgan):
Mike, on the remodel program, how are you measuring ROI and any updates on capex allocation?

Mike Rivera, Chief Financial Officer:
Great question, Alex. ROI is tracked at 3.2x over three years historically, with year-one SSS uplift of +5.8% and margin expansion of 110 bps from premium merchandising and labor efficiencies. We're on track with $292.5 million for 220 remodels this year, scaling to $500 million in FY25 for 300 more. Capex remains organically funded, prioritizing high-AUV flagships and suburban mid-tiers where comps exceed 6%.

Operator:
[Operator Instructions] There are no further questions at this time.

Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
